Midway.wildlife_intro:
Our crew works Midway in Davidson County, where central Piedmont south of Winston-Salem puts woods and water right against housing. Raccoons den in chimneys and attics in spring, squirrels chew soffits year-round, and bats use older rooflines in summer.

Most Midway jobs start with a full roofline, attic, and crawlspace inspection, then removal and sealing as one job, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

Midway is a Davidson County community that never incorporated and never needed to — a crossroads settlement of farmhouses, church streets, and spreading subdivisions midway between Winston-Salem and Lexington, in rolling Piedmont farm country. Its wildlife work is farm-country work moving suburban: raccoons in the farmhouse chimneys and, now, in the subdivision attics at the community's edges; groundhogs in every sunny bank and field edge; skunks under the porches and outbuildings; bats in the older homes; and beavers in the creeks that cross the farmland and flood the low fields from time to time.

The outbuilding is Midway's signature structure. Barns, tobacco barns, well houses, equipment sheds — a Midway farmstead offers an animal more roof options than the house itself, and raccoons and opossums rotate among them through the year. Our Midway inspections survey the whole farmstead, not just the dwelling, because evicting a raccoon from the house attic into the barn loft is a result that lasts about a week.
Midway.extendedBody:
The farmstead survey: house, barns, and everything between

A Midway job starts with a walk of the whole property: house, barns, well house, sheds, and the fence lines. Raccoons den in the barn lofts and take the house chimney in spring; opossums live under the outbuildings and commute to the porches; groundhogs hold the banks behind the barns where the mowing stops. We rank the structures by activity, remove the residents under the depredation-permit system, and seal in an order that leaves the animals no building to rotate into. Every operator is a licensed Wildlife Control Agent with the NC Wildlife Resources Commission — the credential behind the work, and the one to ask any company about.

Groundhogs, banks, and the bat calendar

Groundhog work is Midway's ground constant: burrow systems in the field banks, under the barn foundations, and along the road cuts, with the animals trapped and the active entrances collapsed or screened so the bank is not re-let by June. Bats follow the state calendar — North Carolina prohibits evictions during pup season, May 1 through July 31 — so the big brown colonies in the older farmhouses are inspected and mapped in summer and excluded completely in August, with the layered farmhouse rooflines read gap by gap.

The subdivision edge

Where Midway's new streets meet the farmland, the first calls follow the Stallings pattern at smaller scale: displaced raccoons and armadillos testing new construction, moles in the new lawns laid over old pasture. First-year perimeter inspections on the boundary lots are the cheap version of every one of those calls.
